demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: John, a 54-year-old forester with North American ethnicity, has been struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) since an accident that occurred during his work. The traumatic event happened several months ago when he was working in the forest and accidentally caused serious injury to a colleague. Since then, John has experienced a range of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. The day of the accident is still vivid in John’s mind. He was operating heavy machinery when it suddenly malfunctioned, leading to an incident where his colleague fell from a tree and sustained severe injuries. The physical pain he felt during the event was intense, and now, any experience of bodily discomfort reminds him of that fateful day. Whenever he feels even minor pains or discomforts, John immediately becomes hypervigilant, as if reliving the moment when he caused harm. This trigger intensifies his feelings of threat and danger, making it nearly impossible for him to relax even in safe environments. John’s memories of the event are deeply embedded and often accompanied by a reenactment of physical sensations and emotions. When these memories come flooding back, his body seems to relive the position he was in during the accident. The overwhelming grief that follows each recall is compounded by intense feelings of rage directed at himself for causing the injury. These memories have become intertwined with his triggers, leading him to feel a profound sense of guilt and self-blame. John has come to believe that there is something inherently wrong with him, something that made this event happen. He cannot rely on himself anymore, feeling as though he is no longer capable of performing the tasks that once defined him as a forester. These negative appraisals have further deepened his anxiety and sense of threat from strangers, who now seem like potential sources of danger. John finds himself constantly watching others for signs they might harm him, which only serves to reinforce his feelings of vulnerability. The loop between triggers, memories, and negative appraisals has created a self-perpetuating cycle that feels inescapable. When John encounters physical pain or other reminders of the accident, he becomes hyperalert, which then triggers memories of the event. These memories bring back intense bodily sensations and emotional turmoil, reinforcing his feelings of intrinsic fault and incapability. This reinforcement only exacerbates his sense of threat from others, making it even more difficult for him to feel safe in any environment. John’s wife has noticed a significant change in his behavior over the past few months. He avoids work-related activities that might trigger memories of the accident, leading to tension at home and difficulties in fulfilling his professional responsibilities. The inability to perform his job tasks and maintain relationships has pushed John to seek help. What frightens him most is not just the possibility of another accident but the fear that he will never be able to trust himself again. He hopes for a way to regain control over his life, to find peace with his past actions, and to once again feel capable and in control. John’s current state is marked by intense anxiety and self-doubt, making it clear why this traumatic event has had such a profound impact on him. The combination of triggers, threat responses, memory intrusions, and negative appraisals has formed a vicious cycle that John hopes to break through therapy.
